A horse galloping to the left
Pictograph of a horse.
怒也。武也。象馬頭髦尾四足之形。凡馬之屬皆从馬。

Pictogram (象形) – a horse with its head facing the left, showing a flowing mane in the wind, standing vertically on two legs. In the bronze inscriptions, the head was often simplified into an eye (目 (mù)). The legs eventually evolved into four dots (灬 (huǒ), unrelated to 火 (huǒ)).
Contrast with 鹿 (lù, “deer”), which saw a very different development, and 𢊁 (as in 薦 /荐 (jiàn)), which is a hybrid: it has the legs of 馬 (灬 (huǒ)) but the head of 鹿 (lù).
Wanderwort (Jacques, 2009; Felner and Hill, 2019; Lai et al., 2020). This word is often compared to other Sino-Tibetan forms, e.g., Tibetan རྨང (rmang), Burmese မြင်း (mrang:), Japhug mbro, Tangut 𘆝 (*rjijr¹), Chepang [script needed] (sĕraŋ), Proto-Kuki-Chin *raŋ (> Lai ràŋ) (Benedict, 1972; Schuessler, 2007; STEDT), but the lack of nasal coda in Chinese would be irregular, suggesting borrowing from a sister language rather than common ancestry (Sagart et al., 2019). Outside of Sino-Tibetan, this has also been compared to Mongolian ᠮᠣᠷᠢ (mori), Korean 말 (mal), Japanese 馬(うま) (uma) (Schuessler, 2007; Lai et al., 2020).
The sense of “big” is derived from “horse”; compare the English uses of horse. For the insect prefix sense, see 螞 /蚂. It has converged with the sense of “big”.
The surname is popularly known to be prevalent among Hui Muslims, where it is likely derived from Arabic مُحَمَّد (muḥammad, “Muhammad”), although the surname 馬 itself predates Islam.
From Hokkien 媽 /妈 (má).

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Character Database (中央研究院漢字構形資料庫)
evidence.field: 字形演變; character record 馬, U+99AC
evidence.text: The record presents forms under oracle-bone script, bronze inscriptions (including 集成02594), Chu slips and silk, small seal, and Shuowen. Its account describes 馬 as depicting the whole animal, highlighting its large eye, mane, body, and long tail. This supports a pictograph analysis; the entry does not assign semantic or phonetic roles to subcomponents.
evidence.title: 漢字「馬」：字形演變

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A04619 馬; researched variant entries and cited Shuowen account
evidence.text: The dictionary reports the Shuowen account that the graph depicts the horse’s head, mane, tail, and four legs. It separately describes several variant graphs as later regularized forms of older graphs and notes that a variant graph may become corrupted in transmission. These are claims about variants recorded in that dictionary, not proof that the standardized simplified form 马 descends from any one of those variants.
evidence.title: [A04619] 馬 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: Chinese glyph origin; historical forms; pronunciation and reconstruction tables
evidence.text: The page labels 馬 pictographic and displays historical-form categories for Shang, Western Zhou, Spring and Autumn, Warring States, and Shuowen. It describes later graphic changes including simplification of the head in some bronze forms and stylization of the legs as four dots. Its transcribed Baxter–Sagart table gives Middle Chinese *mæX and Old Chinese *mˤraʔ; a separate Zhengzhang table gives *mraːʔ. These are different reconstruction systems and should not be conflated. The page also reports a proposed “big” extension and surname history, but those are not independently dated in the inspected primary materials here.
evidence.title: 馬 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: The local row gives 馬, Mandarin mǎ, Middle Chinese maeX, Old Chinese *mˤraʔ, gloss “horse,” GSR 0040a, and codepoint U+99AC. This agrees with the Baxter–Sagart notation visible in the inspected Wiktionary reconstruction table. The repository row itself is not an external source or click-through URL.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

The local Unihan rows for 馬 and 马 and the local Baxter–Sagart TSV row were inspected, but local files are not external sources. The official Unicode per-character URLs could not be accessed in this session, so the required click-through verification remains unresolved.

The dossier says 马 is simplified from 馬 following cursive script. The inspected external character-specific sources did not establish that exact derivational pathway or identify the standardization document. Therefore the relationship is best recorded as simplified counterpart only where the source explicitly makes that statement; no component analysis or chronology should be inferred from the shapes alone.

No proposed sound component or phonetic loan is involved in this graph’s pictographic analysis. Comparisons of the spoken word 馬 with other language forms do not by themselves establish the graph’s origin or a borrowing direction; no independent source-word borrowing analysis was completed.
No extract reuse recommendation: the consulted character-specific references add evidence through their individual entries, but no applicable bulk-reuse permission was verified.

No date for the earliest individual 馬 inscription or earliest lexical use was confirmed in the inspected character-specific primary page. The page lists oracle-bone forms but its textual summary does not date them.
No dated attestations for later sense extensions or surname usage were researched in this image-provenance-focused pass; dictionary gloss order is not used to infer chronology.

The evidence supports 馬 as a whole-animal pictograph. No separate semantic or phonetic subcomponents are proposed; the Shuowen component account is historical testimony, not independent confirmation of the exact earliest graphic details.
